short: Alaric's Goths take the city of Rome — the first time in eight hundred years a foreign army had.
full:
Alaric had spent years trying to get what he wanted by negotiation: land for his people and a command in the Roman army. He besieged Rome three times to force the point. Twice the city bought him off. The third time, in August 410, someone opened the Salarian Gate.

The sack itself lasted three days and was, by the standards of ancient warfare, restrained — the Goths were Christians, the great basilicas were spared, and the city was not burned. Materially it mattered less than the loss of Africa's grain a generation later.

What it did was psychological. Rome had not been taken since the Gauls in 390 BCE, and it was still the idea on which the empire's self-understanding rested, even though the western court had moved to Ravenna and the emperor was not there to be captured. Jerome, in Bethlehem, wrote that his voice failed him. Augustine began The City of God in response, arguing that no earthly city was ever the point.
